en: Now, for the sake of accomplishing yoga, one should resort to a soundless place;
it should be well-concealed, frequented by yogins, unbolted, and unguarded. || 1 ||
There, having assumed a yogic posture with the chest expanded,
one should then withdraw the Lord of the Senses from the objects of the senses into the small vessel of the heart.

With the gaze fixed on the tip of the bridge of the nose, while the mind remains established in its all-pervasive state, one should perform the six types of breath control (prāṇāyāma) through the various divisions such as exhalation (recaka) and the rest. || 3 ||
Thereafter, one should maintain the fiery concentration (āgneyī dhāraṇā) in the navel-center,
by which one burns away sins and the effects of [past] actions once one is well-established.
One should always hold the gentle [form] within the heart, which rests upon the moon;
by means of it, one established in the stage of yoga causes nourishment everywhere. 5.
The wise man should bear upon his head the Goddess Īśānī, the sovereign of all,
by whom all yogins attain the supreme state.
The concentration on the nectar (amṛtā-dhāraṇā) is indeed established everywhere;
may it likewise manifest for you here, bestowing the nectar of dharma and knowledge.
Whether smeared with the mire of sin or afflicted by cold, one situated in the Kumbhaka [breath-retention] should practice the seed-syllable and maintain the fire-dhāraṇā. 8.
One should contemplate the seed-syllable of the fire-element (RA), situated within fire and wind, ignited by the fourth vowel, blazing intensely. 9.
One should dry up the supreme water completely with this fire;
then, once it has arisen, one should likewise join it into the subsequent fire.
When that flame-mouthed [fire] is well-pleased and resides within the lunar orb in the heart, one should continuously fill the body with it without obstacle. 11.
Filling the pores of his skin with a mass of smoke-like rays,
he then caused them to fall from his many ears through millions of mouths.
Having filled the entire world with that [sound], it is perceived at the end of the *uddhāta*;
it destroys all sins, both of others and of oneself. || 13 ||
One should maintain this dhāraṇā for the purpose of making things motionless, for the destruction of cold, for the extraction of serpents, and for the subduing of enemies.
One should pierce that which stands in the region of Varuṇa with the second [vowel], as previously described;
the seed-syllable is very gentle, joined with the bindu as before. 15.
One should meditate on this very practice as being face-downward, from the heart down to the knot in the region of Varuṇa, having pierced through the knots. 16.
Therefore, when the fire has been well-extinguished with very bright waters and the Soma has been offered with those same waters,
one should meditate upon the Soma as perfectly stainless.
With his pure rays directed downward toward the circle of the navel,
having destroyed the supreme water, he should establish the supreme water.
Then, when the water has become one, having filled the body as before, it issues forth from the pores of the skin; one should then fill the great universe. 19.
Having meditated thus, at the end of the fourth [breath] he becomes utterly pure;
like a yogi fit for yoga, he shall be one who has exerted himself in the dhāraṇās.
The supreme practitioner, relying on the seed-syllable, should maintain the gentle dhāraṇā during the rite of nourishment, as well as for the removal of poison and in all cases of burning heat. 21.
One should meditate upon the withdrawal (saṃhāra) situated in fire and air, conjoined with the Puruṣa and illuminated by the sixth [vowel]; this is known as the Īśānī dhāraṇā. 22.
Having filled the body with air purified by the fire-dhāraṇā,
one should gradually draw it up from the tips of the big toes and hold it in the head.
Then, with the mind offered to Brahman, one should exhale slowly and continuously through the nostril alone, or else proceed through the path of Brahman (brahmarandhra) toward the Supreme.
One should always sustain the pervasive Amṛtā as the all-pervading one;
when she is thus established, yoga and knowledge are realized.
One should meditate upon oneself and the world as resembling pure crystal,
originating from the Self, heated, and having attained a state of tranquility.
Established on the path of yoga, one who has set out toward the supreme state of mental stability should bring these opposing states to dissolution.
The practitioner [should know] the causes and the prosperity resulting from the perfection of mantras, as well as his own wondrous methods, while remaining intent upon the welfare of others. || 28 ||
Because of that yoga which has ascended, since his state is fixed upon the upper limit, even this common [element], when joined with it, further diminishes [the afflictions]. (29)
Pushing the mental fluctuation that has become established on the path forward, the boat (ūha) proceeds;
having reached the supreme state, the boat turns back from the great flood.
By this, the yogi should discern that entity which, existing in many forms, is the cause of the engagement in and the withdrawal from the accomplishment of yoga. || 31 ||
Meditation (dhyāna) is declared to be the concentration of the mind upon the object that is the meaning of the Śiva-principle;
it is held to be a flow of knowledge whose support is its seed.
Established therein, the yogi attains meditative absorption (samādhi) before long;
once that absorption is fully perfected, he obtains his desired fruit. || 33 ||
Meditating on the object that is the support of consciousness, one should become absorbed in it;
being thus absorbed, one should meditate on non-existence so that the mind becomes supportless.
